To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 3′-CCA end is not an absolute requirement for the aminoacylation of tRNA.
the CCA sequence is not an absolute requirement for aminoacylation of tRNA.
the 3′-end of tRNAs is not an absolute requirement for the tRNA aminoacyl synthetases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and function of tRNAs and their components.
the role of the 3’-CCA end of the tRNA in tRNA aminoacidation.
the role of the CCA sequence of tRNA in the aminoacylation process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tRNAPhe is a good substrate for tRNA amino‐acylation only when the CCA sequence is at the 3’‐end.
the nature of the CCA sequence of tRNA is important for the amino acid specificity of tRNA aminoacyl synthetases.
the 3′ CCA end of tRNA is not an absolute requirement for aminoacylation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 3′ end of tRNAs plays an essential role in tRNA amino acid activation and in the recognition of tRNAs by ribosomes.
the tRNA aminoacyl synthetases recognize the 3′ end of tRNA in a sequence‐dependent way.

the CCA sequence is not a structural requirement for the acceptor activity of tRNAPhenylalanine, although it seems to be an important factor in determining the substrate specificity and efficiency of the tRNA binding to the synthetase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 3′ end of tRNAs is not essential for tRNA amino acid attachment.
tRNA aminoacyl synthetases are able to recognize and aminoacylate the tRNAs that have the 3′ end other than CCA.
the 3′-end of tRNAs can be modified without losing the ability to aminoacylate, suggesting that the CCA end of tRNAs is not essential to the function of tRNAs in protein translation.
